claims.text: A Pulumi package is the unit of versioning and distribution, and the components inside it inherit the package's version.
For a source-based plugin package, the package's version is the Git tag on the repository.
Publishing a source-based package to the Pulumi IDP Private Registry is a two-step flow: apply a semver Git tag, then run `pulumi package publish`.
`pulumi package publish` sends the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and places the package in the Private Registry.

Semver-tagged releases are only required for publishing to the Private Registry; source-based packages referenced directly from a `Pulumi.yaml` file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), even if it is not a valid semantic version.

An executable-based plugin package is distributed as a pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs published to package feeds (npm, PyPI, NuGet, Maven, Go module proxy, or private equivalents).
An executable-based package's version is the version embedded in the published binary and SDKs.
Pulumi Cloud customers can publish executable-based packages to the Private Registry via `pulumi package publish`.
Pulumi recommends defining exactly one package per repository, grouping cohesive components in the package, and using one repository per package.
A repository containing multiple Pulumi packages must either release them in lockstep or invent per-package release tooling that conflicts with how Pulumi consumes packages.
Multiple components inside a single package ship together at the package's version.
The Amazon EKS package in the Pulumi Registry bundles a managed Kubernetes cluster component along with supporting components needed to secure and operate it.
One `PulumiPlugin.yaml` at the repository root defines the package, with components living alongside it.
Bundling unrelated components in one package causes every package release to version every component the same way, which violates semver and forfeits meaningful semantic versioning.
Pulumi does not recommend using a single monorepo containing one giant package for all of an organization's components.
